sweep_summary: Seven title hits for English; none changes the catalog's weight-hedged coding from Hayes 1982. Peck 1971 (Kivung 4(3)) was located in the LLM/Kivung open archive, downloaded (pp. 194-207; pp. 192-193 missing from the scan) and scanned: it is a review of Vanderslice's rules for assigning sentence accent and intonation to text and presupposes dictionary-listed word stress, so it is silent on placement. Peperkamp 1997 (dissertation, print only) and 1996 (Kleinhenz volume, paywalled; Glottolog's '1966'/'Acta Linguistica Hafniensia' are errors) are about prosodic words and clitics in Romance/Dutch, judged from the author's open GLOT 1999 summary and abstracts. Aitken 1984 and Petyt 1985 use 'accent' in the regional-pronunciation sense (not relevant). Pike 1945 (intonation-marking procedure in Fries's ESL manual) is on archive.org only as restricted lending; Hayes 1995 (already listed) has no open copy and would only restate Hayes 1982. No new authoritative stress statement found; nothing to acquire at high priority.

new_statements.quote: Certain multisyllable primary attributives accented on the final syllable in absolute or post-verb position, may be accented on a non[-]final syllable when immediately preceding a subject-head accented on a first syllable. This pattern is almost always maintained in the writer's speech. In the following words the primary attributives immediately preposed to a subject-head with initial stress have the stress on the first syllable. all-wise, biting-cold, bitter-sweet, blood-red, blue-eyed, Chinese, clean-cut, clean-shaven, dead-drunk, dead-tired, deep-set, fourteen [...] unknown, well-done, well-made, wide-open. [...] Before subject-heads with initial unstressed syllable the choice of accentual forms varies.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog row for English (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and no existing statements. Nida adds no placement rule but documents the rhythmic retraction of final-accented attributives before initially-stressed heads (the later 'Rhythm Rule') and the atonic status of determiners, which is compatible with any characterisation of English as having non-fixed, lexically variable word stress. Note that the open link recorded by Glottolog (sil.org/acpub/repository/) is dead; the SIL archives page for 11827 also 404s; the Florida scan on archive.org (synopsisofenglis00nida) is not access-restricted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for the placement of word stress is given (the book is a syntax; the 1960 preface says intonation 'is here treated only under Bloomfield's taxeme of modulation'). What it does record is rhythmic stress retraction: polysyllabic attributives that carry final accent in isolation or after the verb (Chinese, fourteen, dead-drunk, unknown, well-made..) take initial stress when they immediately precede a head noun with initial stress ('a 'Chinese 'bank' vs 'a Chin'ese in'vasion', 'the 'fourteen 'boys' vs 'He was four'teen'); before heads with an initial unstressed syllable the choice varies. It also notes that determiners (my, our, the, a..) are usually atonic except under emphatic or contrastive stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the compound/phrase examples are marked with primary accents only ('a 'Chinese 'bank / a Chin'ese in'vasion').
new_statements.exceptions: Variation before heads whose first syllable is unstressed; the pattern is stated for 'the writer's speech' (American English, 1943 dissertation).
new_statements.identity_note: Brilioth 1913 describes the dialect of Lorton, West Cumberland; Hirst 1906 the dialect of the Kendal district, South Westmorland (Ellis D. 31 variety iii), from a single informant born 1849. Nida 1960 reports 'the writer's speech' (American English; the text is his 1943 Michigan dissertation reissued with a 1960 preface). The five theses concern standard English syntax/semantics.

new_statements.quote: § 244. Short and long vowels as well as diphthongs in unaccented syllables have been weakened into ə, i, or disappeared altogether. These weakenings may be divided into two different groups : A. Weakenings caused by word-stress ; B. Weakenings caused by sentence-stress. To the former group belong chiefly prefixes and suffixes as well as initial, medial, and final syllables preceded or followed by the principal accent ; to the latter enclitic and proclitic words, articles, pronouns, particles, prepositions, and auxiliaries. [p. 67] ... Adverbs of manner and degree. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for where the principal accent falls is stated; the grammar presupposes one 'principal accent' per word and describes its effects: vowels of unaccented syllables (prefixes, suffixes, syllables before or after the principal accent) are reduced to ə, i or lost ('weakenings caused by word-stress'), while enclitic and proclitic words (articles, pronouns, particles, prepositions, auxiliaries) are reduced by sentence stress. The a-prefixes (about, above, again, alone, across..) are unaccented and reduced. Two adverbs in -ly are stressed on the suffix (accordingly, surely; the latter only among old speakers).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated at word level; 'secondary' forms are given only for personal pronouns as sentence-level weak forms (§406, p. 96: 'The secondary and unstressed forms are in parentheses').
new_statements.exceptions: accordingly and surely stressed on the adverbial suffix -ly (p. 130); a-prefixed words with unaccented initial syllable (§245, p. 67).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement of where the main stress falls. The grammar assumes a 'main stress' (also 'chief stress', 'full stress') and a 'secondary stress' per word and uses them as conditioning environments: the vowel [ɔ] (mid-back-wide-round) occurs only in syllables without the main stress; 'the stress h' exists but is absent where original stress has been lost; unrounding of ME. u in 'could', 'should' and the voicing of OE. þ to ð are attributed to secondary stress; several sources of n occur 'only with secondary, or absence of stress'; hw becomes w in unstressed positions. Pronouns have stressed, secondary and unstressed forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is recognised as a distinct degree (§95 p. 46; §270 p. 92 'with secondary, or absence of stress'; §291 p. 96 'in a position of secondary stress (see HES. § 780)'; consonant tables pp. 118-121 'finally with secondary stress'); no rule for its position is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None on placement; pronouns have three sentence-level forms (stressed, secondary, unstressed), §§ 400 ff., pp. 128-129.

Quotes verified against the rendered page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the grammar. The chapters are organised by vowels in accented vs unaccented syllables (Chs. II-III vs Ch. V, §§ 241-249: vowels in unaccented syllables weaken to ə, i or are lost; § 242 lists prefixed words such as befuə(r) 'before', begin, əbat 'about' as having the principal accent on the syllable after the prefix; § 249 gives weak forms of function words governed by the sentence accent). Placement is stated only for particular classes: diphthongs and triphthongs are stressed on their first element (p. 3); the reflexive pronouns mi-sen/-sel/-seln, ði-sen, i-sen, wə-sen etc. carry the stress on the second syllable (§ 353); adverbs of manner in -li are stem-stressed except siuəlĭ 'surely' and əkuədinlái 'accordingly', which stress the suffix (§ 399). In the dialect specimens a raised dot marks a strong stress only where it is not obvious (p. 212).
new_statements.exceptions: Suffix stress in siuəlĭ 'surely' and əkuədinlái 'accordingly' (§ 399, p. 166); § 242 (p. 68) lists edikeet 'educate', kontreeri 'contrary', redzeste(r) 'register', spekteklz 'spectacles' (scanned spellings) as words whose initial syllable is not weakened.
new_statements.identity_note: Wright 1892 describes the Windhill dialect (West Riding of Yorkshire, near Bradford), not Standard English. Fon 2002 and Herman 1998 analyse English spoken by subjects recorded at Ohio State University; the variety is not specified in the pages read. Walrod 2006 is about Philippine languages (Ga'dang, Ilocano, Bontoc, Ifugao, Ibaloi, Tagalog) and is attached to English only by content language. The three SIL book reviews and Dooley 2007 concern English in general (vocabulary, prepositions, word history, discourse topicality).

sources.quote: Lexical stress is an aspect of prosody in multisyllabic words in English and other languages. Lexical stress represents a hierarchy in which syllables of a word are more or less prominent, yielding stress assignments that can be considered primary stress (1), secondary stress (2), or tertiary/unstressed (U). [...] Multisyllabic words typically contain one syllable with primary stress, and the remaining syllables may contain secondary or tertiary stress. In American English, lexical stress can differentiate some word pairs, such as noun and verb forms of “record” or “address.” [...] The noun example /ˈɹɛkɝd/ is an example of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (1–U stress pattern) and is a trochaic stress pattern. In contrast, the verb example of “record” is commonly produced as /ɹəˈkɔɹd/, an iambic stress pattern consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (U–1 stress pattern).

This perceptually salient stress reversal phenomenon manifests in production through a High-tone pitch accent, H* or L+H* in the ToBI annotation system (see Beckman et al. 2005), associated with the syllable that bears secondary stress in the unmarked pronunciation of the word. [...] The rhythmic stress reversal rule (thirtéen → thírteen mén) seems to be indeed the preferred pattern for our participants, in agreement with the predictions of the metrical literature on English phrasal stress. Whereas Grabe and Warren (1995) failed to find robust acoustic evidence for stress shift, our analysis of pitch contours has allowed us to distinguish shifted (Early High) from unshifted (Primary) and Unaccented patterns in production.

sources.quote: Polysyllabic words in English have one syllable that carries primary stress. In some cases, stress is paradigmatic and its placement follows a certain pattern depending on the part of speech (e.g., noun-verb homographs as in PROject vs. proJECT) or the attachment of a stress-shifting derivational suffix (e.g., the suffix -ic causing primary stress to move to the preceding syllable as in HARmony vs. harMOnic). [...] the acoustic correlates of primary stress are mainly duration, intensity, and pitch in both English and Arabic (Almbark et al., 2014).

sources.quote: Generally speaking, the modern metrical structure of the three languages is trochaic (i.e. stress falls on the left). If a word has two light syllables, then stress is primarily trochaic for all three languages. If a word has two heavy syllables (i.e. syllables with long vowels or are closed by a coda consonant), then Dutch and German prefer stress on the second syllable, while English prefers the leftmost syllable, although there can be variation. If the first syllable is light and the second clearly heavy, which is rare for English, stress falls on the final syllable. Some later loans do have a final heavy syllable in English which can bear stress. There is a strong tendency for English to have main stress on the first syllable e.g. costume ['kɒstjuːm] while the German word is stressed finally, Kostüm [kɔs'ty:m].

sources.quote: The English language has free word stress (O‘Connor, 1973, p. 233) which means the ―stress can be in anywhere in a word; there is no single position where the stress of a word can be expected to fall in English‖ (Quirk et al., 1985, p. 1590). For example, counting from left to right, it may fall on the: 1st vowel: SYnonym 2nd vowel: caNAry 3rd vowel: evaNESCE 4th vowel: responsiBIlity 5th vowel: osteopoROsis 6th vowel: industrialiZAtion [...] The rule states that if the word ending is preceded by two or more consecutive consonants, the stress may fall on the vowel right before these consonants. If the ending is preceded by only one consonant or one vowel, then the stress may fall on the second vowel before the ending, if the word is long enough to have two vowels before the ending. If the word has only two vowels i.e. two-syllable words, then the stress will fall on the second vowel from the end, that is, the first syllable of the word (Waldo, 1968, p. 36).

sources.quote: Main stress nearly always falls on one of the final three syllables of a word, and within that three-syllable window both heavy penultimate syllables and heavy final syllables can attract main stress. ... When the penult is definitely light (V), antepenultimate stress is the clear preference: penultimate stress appears in just 21% of cases. ... Specifically, a final [i] pushes main stress leftwards – in three-syllable words this means that stress has a strong tendency to be antepenultimate. sources.quote: Although English has been mentioned among the languages which do not exhibit an interaction of stress with either the onset quality or the presence of an onset, this study reveals that the distribution of onsetless syllables is correlated with the position of stress. First, stressed syllables support not only more complex onsets in terms of length but also a greater array of consonant clusters. Weak syllables, in turn, repel clusters and favour empty onsets or onsets composed of a singleton consonant. Second, the proximity to the stressed syllable also shows to be a predictor of onset complexity; a variety of complex onsets increases as the distance towards the stressed syllable decreases.

sources.quote: In two-syllable words, if a word is a noun, stress has to be on the first syllable e.g. c'onvert and if it is a verb, stress has to be on the second syllable e.g., Conv'ert. In three-syllable words, if the final syllable of verbs is strong, it has to carry stress: e.g., enter'tain. If the last syllable is weak, the stress has to be on the preceding (penultimate) syllable e.g. de'termine. If both the second and the third syllables are weak, the initial syllable carries stress e.g. 'parody. [...] Stress in English is variable whereas stress in Arabic is fixed.

sources.quote: English is a stress language. In multiple-syllable words, a certain syllable is produced more prominently than others. However, English stress patterns are not as predictable as fixed-stress languages such as French. Yet, certain patterns can also be observed. Generally, there is a difference between nouns and verbs in terms of lexical stress. For nouns, if the penultimate syllable is heavy, it is stressed; otherwise the antepenultimate syllable is stressed (McMahon, 2002). A heavy syllable is defined as one with a branching rhyme, that is, with a tense vowel (long or diphthong) or a vowel plus coda.

sources.quote: The main active rule is the so-called Latin stress rule (Halle and Vergnaud 1987), which, despite the name, also applies to many English polysyllabic words. This rule codifies the generalization that heavy syllables tend to attract stress. Below is a description of this, divided into four subrules: If the penultimate syllable is light, the antepenultimate syllable is stressed. If the penultimate syllable is heavy, it is stressed. In the case of disyllabic words, the first syllable is stressed. Monosyllabic words are stressed. Despite the descriptive power of the generalization, examples exist of words where it fails, such as an|te|nna, a|la|ba|ma or po|lice. [Heavy syllable: The syllable has a coda or ends in a tense vowel. Light syllable: Any syllable not classified as heavy.]

sources.citation: Hong, Sung-Hoon. 2016. A Noisy Harmonic Grammar analysis of English vowel reduction in stress clash environments. Studies in Phonetics, Phonology and Morphology 22(2): 399-422. doi:10.17959/sppm.2016.22.2.399

sources.quote: In English, there is a strong tendency to avoid two adjacent stresses. One common strategy is to destress one of the clashing stresses and shift it to a syllable nearby. Such resolution of stress clashes may occur between two stressed syllables across a word boundary (e.g. antíque > àntique cháir) or within a word across a morpheme boundary (e.g. Japán > Jàpan-ése, adóre > àdor-átion). Along with clash avoidance, there is another robust tendency to consider, cyclic stress preservation (Chomsky and Halle 1968), whereby the stress assigned in an earlier cycle is preserved in the next cycle (e.g. [condénse] > [còndèns]átion]). Thus, when the main stress of a derivative falls next to the stress of a base, the contexts for both stress preservation and clash avoidance are met, and either of the two phenomena could potentially take place.

sources.quote: This paper examines factors affecting vowel reduction that occurs in the environment of stress clash. sources.quote: English is a stress-timed language. All content words of an utterance are produced with main stress; determiners, auxiliaries, and the like are typically unstressed. When words are comprised of more than one syllable, main stress occurs on just one of these. Thus, in disyllabic words, stress either occurs on the first syllable or on the second and so these words are produced with either a trochaic or iambic stress pattern. That said, the most frequent location for word stress in English is on the first syllable (Cutler & Carter, 1987). [...] English is also a quantity sensitive language, meaning that lexical stress is correlated with syllable structure. So-called heavy syllables, which have either long vowel nuclei (tense vowels or diphthongs) or final consonants, are more likely to have stress than light syllables, which have a short vowel nuclei (i.e., lax vowels; Hayes, 1995). [...] disyllabic nouns are usually stressed on the first syllable, while disyllabic verbs are more often stressed on the second.

sources.locator: sec. 6 Production of Word Stress, Table 6 (pp. 7-8) and p. 8
sources.note: An L2 interlanguage study: 20 Chadian student-teachers of English (L1s French and Arabic, some also Gambai, Sara, Fulfulde or Tupuri) read 80 test words that were audio-recorded and transcribed by ear against General British, and most of them stressed nearly every syllable (′Wed ′nes ′day, u ′ni ′ver ′sity), which the author attributes to French syllable timing. On English itself the article only restates the GB reference forms and two suffix rules (-ation penultimate, -ity/-phy antepenultimate), so it adds nothing to, and does not contradict, the catalog's Hayes-based entry for English.

sources.citation: Veronica, Siska, Syafrizal Sabaruddin & Indah Damayanti. 2018. An Analysis on English Syllable Stress Placements of the English Study Program Students. Journal of English Education and Teaching 2(1): 51-58. doi:10.33369/jeet.2.1.51-58
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: A written test of English word-stress placement (10 items per syllable-count type, high-frequency words) given to 49 Indonesian English-education students at Bengkulu University found low knowledge overall (mean 39.3/100), with the most errors on 4-syllable words ending in -ion, -ty, -ry and many second- and fourth-semester students choosing answers with stress on both syllables of disyllables. It reports learner scores only, with no acoustic measurement and no statement of where English word stress falls or of the weight-sensitivity the catalog entry records.
sources.venue: Journal of English Education and Teaching

sources.citation: Wilhelm, Stephan. 2018. Tradition et changement phonétique dans une variété de contact : l’anglais de Lewis et Harris. Corela 16(1). doi:10.4000/corela.6623
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: The article describes the traditional Hebridean English accent of Lewis and Harris (vowels, rhoticity, /x/, retroflexion, intonation, voice quality) and apparent-time change among adolescents through dialect levelling and the decline of Gaelic. Its only suprasegmental content is sentence intonation (a default rise-fall nuclear tone, occasional rise-slump, the Urban North British Intonation system) and voice quality; it says nothing about word stress or lexical tone, so it neither confirms nor changes the English entry.

sources.citation: Akindele, Julianah A. 2017. Phonetic Quantity Cue in the English of Educated Edo Nigerians as Reflection of Non-Native English. Traduction et Langues 16(1): 255-267. doi:10.52919/translang.v16i1.632
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: The article studies English as a second language spoken by 300 educated Edo Nigerians and finds that they almost never (4.2%) reduce the final syllabic consonant of words like comfortable and produce all syllables with about the same weight, whereas the two native baselines weaken it every time. It says nothing about where English word stress falls; its only statement about native English is that unstressed final syllabic consonants are weakened and short, so it neither adds to nor challenges the catalog's Hayes-based entry.

sources.citation: Akindele, Julianah. 2017. Stressed and Unstressed Syllable Alternation in Educated Edo (Nigerian) English. Journal of Language and Education 3(4): 52-59. doi:10.17323/2411-7390-2017-3-4-52-59

sources.note: The article finds that educated Edo (Nigerian) second-language speakers of English almost never (11.6% of 6,000 instances) alternate stressed and unstressed syllables in connected-speech rhythm units the way two Standard British English speakers do, instead making nearly every syllable prominent, which the author takes as re-confirming that Nigerian English is syllable-timed rather than stress-timed. It is about L2 rhythm in connected speech and states nothing about the position or type of English word stress, so it does not bear on the catalog's English entry (Hayes 1982, weight-hedged); the…

sources.citation: Arienintya, Dhinar. 2017. The Influence of L1 and L2 in English Stress Shift Production of the EFL Learners in Indonesia. KnE Social Sciences 1(3): 482-488. doi:10.18502/kss.v1i3.770
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: A descriptive L2 study: 33 Indonesian EFL freshmen at Universitas Negeri Malang filled a questionnaire and were recorded reading a 365-word text aloud, and the author scored how many words got the correct English stress, with accuracy falling as syllable count rises. It reports learner accuracy only, never states where English stress falls or by what rule, and makes no acoustic measurement, so it adds nothing to the English entry.

sources.citation: Ashby, Michael & Patricia Ashby. 2017. Unruly intonation. Linguistica 57(1): 29-43. doi:10.4312/linguistica.57.1.29-43
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Three expert judges notated the intonation of a 160-word English test dialogue and agreed closely on phrasing, nucleus placement and nuclear tone, yet the textbook rules of English intonation account for only part of their choices. The paper is about sentence intonation for EFL teaching; it says nothing about English word-stress position or lexical tone, so it neither supports nor changes the catalog entry.

sources.citation: Brēde, Maija. 2017. Phonetic Attributes of Political Discourse. Baltic Journal of English Language, Literature and Culture 7: 26-39. doi:10.22364/bjellc.07.2017.02
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: p. 34, section 3.5 Prominence on function words
sources.note: An auditory (ear-transcribed, not instrumental) analysis of one 41-minute David Cameron speech: it counts nuclear tones per tone unit (final catalog record% low falls, 42.1% high/mid falls; non-final catalog record.1% rises, 30% high/mid falls, 15.6% low falls), pausing, a 'special rise' on numerals, and phrase-level stress placed on function words and half-accented content words for rhythm. It describes intonation and sentence prominence in English public speaking and states nothing about word-stress placement, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog's English word-stress entry.
sources.venue: Baltic Journal of English Language, Literature and Culture

sources.citation: Hong, Jhao-Nan & James H. Yang. 2017. Developing a Pronunciation Computer Program for the Acquisition of English Phonemes and Word Stress. Research in Language 15(4): 325-352. doi:10.1515/rela-2017-0019

sources.note: An L2 pedagogy study: a Flash/Android pronunciation program taught Taiwanese remedial-English students suffix-based English stress rules, and stress-misplacement rates on -ic and -ity words fell from 66.7% to 29.2% and 70.8% to 45.8% between pretest and posttest. The only statements about English stress placement are a textbook suffix table quoted from Liao (2012) and a Ladefoged citation that stress is predictable in most English words; the data are learner productions, so nothing here describes native English stress placement or type independently of the catalog's Hayes 1982 entry.

sources.citation: Kivistö-de Souza, Hanna. 2017. Examining L1 Brazilian Portuguese speakers' sensitivity to English nuclear stress assignment. Revista de Estudos da Linguagem 25(2): 483-514. doi:10.17851/2237-2083.25.2.483-514

sources.note: The article treats sentence-level nuclear stress (tonicity), not word stress: English places nuclear stress on the last stressed syllable of the intonation phrase by default, shifted leftward by the Germanic Nuclear Stress Rule (thetic unaccusatives stress the subject) and the Anaphoric Deaccenting Rule (function words and given information are deaccented). The perception test found Brazilian Portuguese learners far less sensitive than native listeners (76% on function-word-final, 52% given-information, 40% unaccusative trials); nothing is stated about word-stress position, weight or type, so…

sources.citation: Luchini, Pedro Luis. 2017. Measurement for accentedness, pause frequency/duration and nuclear stress placement in the EFL classroom. Ilha do Desterro 70(3): 185-200. doi:10.5007/2175-8026.2017v70n3p185
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: An EFL teaching experiment: 50 Spanish-L1 trainee teachers in two groups, and the group given an added awareness-building communicative component improved more in rated accentedness, pause frequency/duration and nuclear stress placement. The only stress statement is the textbook rule that English nuclear (sentence) stress falls on the last lexical content word of a tone unit; nothing on word-stress position, weight or tone.

sources.citation: Rojczyk, Arkadiusz & Porzuczek, Andrzej. 2017. Discrimination of English tone contours by Polish learners. Linguistica Silesiana 38: 53-66. doi:10.24425/linsi.2017.117040
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: pp. 53 (abstract), 55 (section 2, Stimuli)
sources.note: An L2 perception experiment: 67 Polish English-studies majors identified English intonation contours (fall, rise, rise-fall, fall-rise on yes/no/good/bad) at 54% and discriminated them in an AXB task at 92% (d' 2.67), so the authors conclude the learners' difficulty is with labelling, not with hearing the contours. 'Tone' in the title means intonational nuclear tone on a monosyllable, not lexical tone; the paper states nothing about English word stress or lexical tone, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog entry (weight-hedged stress, no-tone).

sources.citation: Chubarova, Yulia & Rezepova, Natalia. 2016. Discourse Elements in English Academic Discourse. Journal of Language and Education 2(1): 56-64. doi:10.17323/2411-7390-2016-2-1-56-64
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Auditory (perceptual) analysis of the intonation of discourse elements such as so, well, you know and I mean in six recorded lectures by three General American speakers: the elements mostly form their own intonation group and take Medium Level or Low Rise terminal tones with average tempo and loudness. The article is about phrase-level intonation and says nothing about word stress or lexical tone.

sources.citation: Chen, Jin, Jianghao Lin & Xinguang Li. 2015. The Validity and Reliability of Rhythm Measurements in Automatically Scoring the English Rhythm Proficiency of Chinese EFL Learners. English Language Teaching 8(6): 80-88. doi:10.5539/elt.v8n6p80
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: The article measures sentence-level timing (vowel and consonant interval variability) in English read by Chinese learners against five British speakers and finds that dV, dC, VarcoV, nPVI and rPVI separate native speakers from three learner levels (native highest, falling with proficiency), with an autoscore correlating.866 with teacher ratings. On English word stress it only repeats textbook statements that English rhythm is stress-timed and stress-based, without stating any stress position or type, so it adds nothing to the catalog entry.

sources.citation: Gralińska-Brawata, Anna. 2015. The Relationship Between English and Polish Rhythm Measures in Polish Learners of English. Research in Language 13(2): 124-139. doi:10.1515/rela-2015-0020
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: p. 125, section 2 'Rhythm in English and in Polish'
sources.note: The article measures the durational rhythm of L2 English and L1 Polish in the same 30 Polish learners and finds that most rhythm measures correlate between the two languages within speakers, most strongly %V and ΔC at fast tempo. It says nothing about where English word stress falls; its only stress remark is the received characterisation of English as stress-timed with a variable stress pattern and vowel reduction, cited from Abercrombie, Dauer and Laver.

sources.citation: Patel, Rupal, Kevin J. Reilly, Erin Archibald, Shanqing Cai & Frank H. Guenther. 2015. Responses to Intensity-Shifted Auditory Feedback During Running Speech. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research 58(6): 1687-1694. doi:10.1044/2015_JSLHR-S-15-0164

sources.note: American English speakers whose auditory feedback was made quieter on the emphatically stressed word of a short sentence raised the intensity difference between the stressed and unstressed word; speakers whose feedback was made louder did not change, and F0 and duration did not change significantly for either group. The article is about sentence-level emphatic stress on monosyllables and speech motor control, and says nothing about where word stress falls in English or what kind of system it is.
sources.venue: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research

sources.citation: Banzina, Elina, Lynne E. Hewitt & Laura C. Dilley. 2014. Using synchronous speech to facilitate acquisition of English rhythm: A small-scale study. EuroAmerican Journal of Applied Linguistics and Languages 1(1): 69-84. doi:10.21283/2376905x.1.9

Nothing is measured acoustically and the only sentence on English stress is a textbook background line on its phonetic correlates, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog entry.

It concerns sentence-level prominence of English function words in learner speech and says nothing about English word-stress placement or type, so it does not bea…

sources.note: An auditive (ear-based, not instrumental) study of sentence intonation in three speakers from a Sky News press-preview discussion: pauses, tempo, timbre, and nuclear tones, with falling tones dominating final tone units and rises more common in non-final ones (Tables 1-2, p. 28). It says nothing about the position or type of English word stress and nothing about lexical tone, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog entry.

sources.citation: Gries, Stefan Th. & Miglio, Viola G. 2014. New information in naturalistic data is also signalled by pitch movement: An analysis from monolingual English/Spanish and bilingual Spanish speakers. Complutense Journal of English Studies 22: 11-33. doi:10.5209/rev_CJES.2014.v22.46957

sources.locator: p. 14; see also p. 26: "both in English and Spanish the main pitch accent in an utterance (also called phrasal or nuclear stress) can fall on the rightmost con…
sources.note: The article is about sentence-level intonation: contour tones (pitch movement) on a noun mark it as new rather than given information, and longer stressed vowels are more likely to carry pitch movement, in California English as in the two Spanish groups. It says only in passing that English has lexical stress and that nuclear stress position is freer than in Spanish; it states nothing about word-stress position or type that bears on the catalog entry.

sources.citation: Kim, Ji-Eun. 2014. A Study on Realizations of English Stress and Vowel Formant Frequency by Korean Learners. Phonetics and Speech Sciences 6(1): 39-45. doi:10.13064/ksss.2014.6.1.039

sources.note: The article measures vowel formants of Korean learners' L2 English and finds that they merge tense and lax stressed front vowels in paragraph reading, have a smaller stressed-vowel space than in frame sentences, and produce unstressed vowels with formants close to native values. Its only statements about English stress itself are textbook background on phonetic correlates and vowel reduction, with no finding on stress placement, so it adds nothing to the weight-hedged entry.

sources.citation: Kim, Ji-Eun. 2014. A Study on the Relation among English Speech Rate, Pitch and Stress by Korean Speakers. Phonetics and Speech Sciences 6(3): 101-108. doi:10.13064/ksss.2014.6.3.101
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: p. 101 (abstract); method p. 102; Tables 4-5 pp. 104-105; conclusion p. 107
sources.note: An L2 study: it measures how Korean learners realize English stressed versus unstressed vowels (duration, F1/F2) and finds this relates to their speech rate but not to their sentence pitch range, which stays under half a cited native figure. It records no native English speakers and states nothing about where English word stress falls or how it is assigned, so it neither confirms nor challenges the catalog entry; the stressed/unstressed labels of the passage are taken as given.

sources.citation: Baba, Ricardo. 2013. Teaching Proper English to Malaysian Speakers: Focusing on the Vowels, Consonants, Syllable, and Stress. US-China Foreign Language 11(4): 279-285. doi:10.17265/1539-8080/2013.04.002

sources.note: An anecdotal pedagogy piece by a business-faculty author on how Malaysian speakers mispronounce English (vowels, consonants, syllabification, stress) and how he teaches them, plus an 80-form course-evaluation survey; there is no measurement and no statement of an English stress rule, only a handful of example words with idiosyncratic apostrophe marks (some, like econoMIST, do not match standard English). Nothing usable for the English entry.

sources.citation: Chen, Wenkai. 2013. An Empirical Study on the Acquisition of English Rising Tone by Chinese EFL Learners. English Language Teaching 6(6): 97-102. doi:10.5539/elt.v6n6p97
sources.tag: read: silent on stress

sources.note: An L2 study of sentence-level rising intonation on general questions: Chinese learners replace the rise by a fall, fail to hold the nucleus pitch, add a schwa after a final consonant, and shift the accent of multisyllabic nuclei (information) to the first syllable. It states that English is an intonation language and not a tone language, which matches the catalog's no-tone class, but gives no word-stress rule beyond the stimulus words' accent positions.

sources.citation: Kouega, Jean-Paul. 2013. RP and the Cameroon English Accent: An Overview. US-China Foreign Language 11(12): 887-900. doi:10.17265/1539-8080/2013.12.001
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: p. 898 (Conclusions); the only stress mention is p. 893: 'Vowel reduction in native Englishes replaces a peripheral vowel or a potential diphthong by the weak…
sources.note: The article is a segmental survey of the Cameroon English accent against RP (vowels, consonants, voicing, clusters, spelling pronunciation) based on auditory analysis of recordings of educated Anglophone Cameroonians; it makes no statement about word-stress placement or type. Table 7 (p. 893, 'Syllabification in CamE') incidentally prints stress marks on CamE forms that differ from RP (e.g. libera'lais, we'nEsde, apo'kop, anihi'let, ma'taja vs. RP initial stress) but the text discusses only the change in syllable count, so nothing bears on the catalog's English entry.

sources.citation: Okazaki, Masao. 2013. Topicalization and Stress Clash Avoidance in the History of English [review of Augustin Speyer, 2010, De Gruyter Mouton]. English Linguistics 30(1): 439-450. doi:10.9793/elsj.30.1_439
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: A book review of Speyer (2010) arguing about whether a Clash Avoidance Requirement on adjacent sentence stresses (full-NP subjects stressed, pronouns stressless) explains the decline of object topicalization from Old English to Present-Day English; the only stress facts given are phrase-level Rhythm Rule shifts and phonological-phrase blocking cited from Hayes (1984, 1989), with no measurement. It states no word-stress rule, position or type for English, so it neither confirms nor challenges the catalog's weight-hedged entry.

sources.citation: Ploquin, Marie. 2013. Prosodic Transfer: From Chinese Lexical tone to English Pitch Accent. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 4(1): 68-77. doi:10.7575/aiac.alls.v.4n.1p.68
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.locator: p. 68 (abstract); p. 69
sources.note: English is treated as a non-tone language whose pitch accents sit on stressed syllables, which matches the entry's no-tone class; the study says nothing about where word stress falls (the target word is a monosyllable). Its finding is about L2 English: the Chinese speakers produced the rising pitch accents on 'fan' with the contour and pitch range of their tone 2, while the falling accents were inconclusive.
sources.venue: Advances in Language and Literary Studies

sources.citation: DiGirolamo, Cara M. 2012. The Fandom Pairing Name: Blends and the Phonology-Orthography Interface. Names 60(4): 231-243. doi:10.1179/0027773812Z.00000000034
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: The article analyses the morphology of English name blends (Internet fandom pairing names such as Drarry, Brangelina) and finds that a blend carries a single primary stress, with the stress peak of one stem aligned to a stress peak of the other in 86.5 percent of the data (Stress Match), alongside onset-complexity and overlap constraints. It states nothing about the English word-stress rule or its weight sensitivity, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog entry; the stress content is a constraint on blend formation only.

sources.citation: Hirst, Daniel. 2012. A tribute to Wiktor Jassem on the occasion of his 90th birthday. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(2): 246-250. doi:10.1017/S0025100312000126
sources.tag: read: silent on stress

sources.note: An IPA NEWS tribute that reprints Jassem's 1949 note on transcribing speech rhythm in educated Southern English: stressed syllables are shortened by following unstressed syllables only when those belong to the same rhythm unit, and unstressed syllables before the rhythmical stress (the anacrusis) are pronounced as short as possible. It concerns phrase-level rhythm units, anacrusis and juncture, states no word-stress placement rule and reports no measurements, so it neither confirms nor challenges the catalog's weight-hedged entry.

The study concerns sentence-level emphatic stress on monosyllabic words and states nothing about where word stress falls in English, its weight sensitivity, or tone, so it neither confirms nor challenges the catalog entry.

It assumes English has stressed and reduced unstressed vowels but states nothing about stress position, weight sensitivity or tone, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog entry.

The paper concerns sentence stress (nuclear tone placement), terminal contours and key in learner English, and states nothing about the position or type of word stress in English or about Serbian prosody, so it does not bear on the catalog entry.

sources.quote: p. 200: "Many other words have two heavy syllables, only one of which is accentable. The following words have two heavy syllables, the second one of which is ordinarily unaccentable. These are called 'falling stress' words. 'ver_ti,go 'ob_fus,cate 'can,not 'fruc_ti,fy 'black,bird 'op_e,ra_tor 'nit,wit 'sky,scra_per. In the following words, the first heavy syllable is unaccentable. Such words are called 'rising stress' words. ,com_pen'sa_tion ,ob_ser'va_tion ,con_fi_gu'ra_tion ,or_ien'ta_tion" — p. 204: "the canonical forms of the words could have been obtained from a dictionary."
sources.locator: p. 200 (Rule IIE, rhythm rule) and p. 204
sources.note: A review article presenting Vanderslice's rules for assigning sentence-level ACCENT, CADENCE, ENDGLIDE, rhythm-rule reduction and de-accenting of echoic elements to running text (an early text-to-speech prosody algorithm). Word-level stress is taken as given: each word's 'canonical form' (heavy accentable / heavy unaccentable / light syllables, 'falling stress' vs 'rising stress' words) is assumed to come from a dictionary; no rule for where lexical stress falls is stated. Archive scan holds pp. 194-207 (pp. 192-193 missing; title block pasted onto p. 194); scanned.
